lessons.title: Indexes and Performance
lessons.focus: How indexes speed up queries and when they slow things down

data.title: Indexes and Performance
data.summary: Indexes are data structures that let databases find rows faster, and they can also affect how quickly data is written. This lesson explains when indexes improve query speed and when they can slow down operations.
objectives: Explain how an index works to speed up data retrieval
Identify queries that benefit from indexes
Recognize situations where indexes can degrade performance
Choose appropriate columns to index for a given query
Describe the trade‑offs between read and write performance
data.prerequisites: Students should already understand basic SQL queries, tables, and primary keys from earlier lessons.
why: In real applications, fast query response times are critical for user satisfaction and business decisions; indexes are one of the main tools to achieve this.
However, indexes also consume storage and slow down INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations, so knowing when to use them prevents hidden performance problems.

sections.heading: What Is an Index?
sections.body:
An index in a database is a **separate data structure** that stores the values of one or more columns in a sorted, searchable order.  
Think of it as a tiny, extra copy of part of the table that is arranged so the database can find rows quickly, without scanning every row.

> **Definition:** An index is a supplemental structure that holds column values (or combinations of values) in a defined order, together with pointers that tell the system where the full rows are stored.

Why does this help?  
A table without an index is like a list of names written on a single sheet of paper. If you want to locate a specific name, you must read the paper line by line until you find it. This is called a **full table scan** and its cost grows directly with the number of rows: if there are 1 000 rows, you may have to look at up to 1 000 entries; if there are 1 million rows, you may have to look at up to 1 million entries.

An index changes the situation. By keeping the indexed column values in order (for example, alphabetical order for text, numeric order for numbers), the database can jump directly to the part of the index where the desired value should appear. This is similar to using **binary search**, which repeatedly halves the search space. The time needed to locate a value in a sorted list of *n* items is roughly $$\log_2 n$$ steps, far fewer than *n* steps for a linear scan.

> **Note:** The index does not store the whole row; it stores just enough information (usually the indexed column value and a pointer) to locate the full row in the main table.

### Everyday comparison

Imagine a textbook with a back‑of‑the‑book index. The index lists important words alphabetically and tells you the page numbers where each word appears. If you want to find every discussion of “photosynthesis,” you look up the word in the index, see the page numbers, and turn directly to those pages. You do not read the entire book page by page. The book’s index is a tiny, ordered list that points to the larger content—exactly what a database index does for a table.

> **In daily life:** A library catalog is another example. The catalog is sorted by title or author and contains a reference (call number) to the shelf location of each book. The catalog lets you locate a book quickly without walking through every aisle.

### How the index is stored

Most relational databases use a **B‑tree** (balanced tree) structure for indexes. A B‑tree is a hierarchy of nodes where each node holds a range of values and pointers to child nodes. The tree stays balanced, meaning every leaf node is at the same depth, so the number of steps from the root to any leaf is the same. This guarantees the $$\log_2 n$$ search cost mentioned earlier.

When you query the database with a condition like `WHERE last_name = 'Smith'`, the engine can:

1. Look up “Smith” in the index (a fast, ordered search).  
2. Follow the pointer(s) stored with “Smith” to the exact row(s) in the main table.  

Only the matching rows are read, saving time and I/O (input/output) operations.

> **Remember:** An index is useful when you frequently search, sort, or join on the indexed column(s). It is less helpful for columns that are rarely used in queries.

### What the index does not do

An index does **not** replace the original table. The table still holds the complete rows, and the index merely provides a shortcut. Because the index is a separate structure, the database must keep it **synchronized** with the table: whenever a row is inserted, updated, or deleted, the corresponding entry in the index must be added, changed, or removed. This extra work is the price you pay for faster reads.

> **Common mistake:** Assuming that adding an index will always improve performance. If a column is rarely used in search conditions, the index adds overhead without benefit, especially for write‑heavy workloads.

In summary, an index is a sorted, auxiliary list that points back to the full rows of a table. By organizing column values in order, it enables the database to locate data with far fewer steps than scanning the whole table, just as a book’s index lets you jump straight to the relevant pages. Understanding this basic idea prepares you for the next topics: how indexes speed up searches, the different kinds of indexes, and when they might slow down writes.

sections.heading: How Indexes Speed Up Searches
sections.body:
Imagine you have a huge phone book that contains millions of names. If you want to find the phone number for **Alice Anderson**, you could flip through every page until you spot her name – that would take a long time.  
Instead, you open the alphabetic index at the back, jump straight to the “A” section, and then scan a few entries until you reach **Alice Anderson**. The index tells you exactly where to look, so you avoid reading the whole book.

> **In daily life:** An index in a book works the same way – it maps a keyword (the word you’re looking for) to the page numbers where that word appears.

A database index works on the same principle. A table is like the phone book: it stores rows (records) one after another. Without an index, the database must perform a **full table scan**, reading every row and checking whether it matches the search condition. This is O(N) work, meaning the time grows linearly with the number of rows N.  

When an index exists, the database can use a **B‑tree** (balanced tree) structure to locate the matching rows. A B‑tree is a special kind of tree where each node can hold many keys and children, keeping the tree shallow even for very large data sets. The depth of the tree is roughly $$\log_{m} N$$ where *m* is the average number of keys per node. Because the tree is shallow, the database needs only a few steps (usually 2–4) to reach the exact location of the desired value.

> **Definition:** A **B‑tree** is a balanced search tree that stores sorted keys in nodes, each node containing multiple keys and child pointers, allowing fast lookup, insertion, and deletion.

### Step‑by‑step lookup with a B‑tree index

1. **Start at the root node.** The root holds a small set of key ranges, for example:  
   `10‑20`, `30‑40`, `50‑60`.  
   If you are looking for the value `37`, you see that it falls in the `30‑40` range, so you follow the pointer to that child node.

2. **Move to the next level.** The child node might contain more precise ranges, such as `31‑35`, `36‑38`, `39‑40`. Since `37` lies in `36‑38`, you follow that pointer.

3. **Reach a leaf node.** Leaves store the actual index entries: the key value (`37`) and a **row identifier** (often called a **row ID** or **pointer**) that tells the database where the full row lives on disk.

4. **Fetch the row.** Using the row identifier, the database jumps directly to the storage location of that row and reads it. No other rows are examined.

Because each step narrows the search dramatically, the total work is proportional to the height of the tree, not the total number of rows. For a table with 10 million rows and a typical B‑tree branching factor of 100, the height is only about 3:

$$\text{height} \approx \log_{100}(10\,000\,000) \approx 3$$

Thus the database reads at most three index pages plus the final data page – a huge saving compared with scanning 10 million rows.

> **Note:** The index stores the key values **in sorted order**, which is why the database can decide which branch to follow at each node.

### Why sorting matters

Sorting the keys lets the B‑tree perform a **binary‑like search** at each node: it can compare the search key with the middle key of the node and decide whether to go left or right, halving the possibilities each time. Even though a B‑tree node holds many keys, the same principle applies – the node’s internal array is searched quickly (often with a small linear scan because the node fits in memory).

### The benefit for different query types

- **Equality search** (`WHERE id = 123`) – the index points directly to the matching row(s).  
- **Range search** (`WHERE date BETWEEN '2023‑01‑01' AND '2023‑01‑31'`) – the index lets the database locate the first row in the range and then walk forward through the leaf nodes, reading only the rows that satisfy the condition.  

In both cases, the database avoids touching rows that are outside the search criteria.

> **Remember:** An index speeds up reads by turning a linear scan (O(N)) into a logarithmic lookup (O(log N)), plus a single direct fetch of the needed row(s). This is why well‑chosen indexes are essential for good query performance.

sections.heading: Types of Indexes
sections.body:
Imagine you have a huge phone book and you want to find a single name quickly.  
If the book is just a long list of names in alphabetical order, you could flip through page after page until you see the one you need – that works, but it can be slow when the book has millions of entries.  
An **index** is a special shortcut that tells the database where to look without scanning everything. Different kinds of shortcuts work better for different kinds of searches, just like different tools are better for different jobs around the house.

### B‑tree index  

A **B‑tree** (short for *balanced tree*) is the most common index type in relational databases.  
Think of a B‑tree as a multi‑level table of contents. The top level lists broad ranges (e.g., A‑F, G‑M, N‑Z). Each of those ranges points to a lower‑level page that splits the range again, and this continues until you reach the exact page where the wanted record lives. Because the tree is *balanced*, every path from the top to a leaf has the same length, so the number of steps needed to find any value is predictable.

Why does this help?  
When you search for a value, the database follows the branches from the root down to a leaf, comparing the search key with the values stored at each node. Each comparison eliminates a large chunk of the data, so you usually need only **log₂(N)** steps, where *N* is the number of rows. For a table with one million rows, a B‑tree might need only about 3‑4 steps.

> **Definition:** A B‑tree index stores keys in a hierarchical, balanced structure that allows fast lookup, insertion, and deletion with logarithmic cost.

**When to use it:**  
- Equality searches (`WHERE id = 123`)  
- Range searches (`WHERE price BETWEEN 10 AND 20`)  
- Sorting results (`ORDER BY column`)  

Because the tree keeps the keys in order, the database can also read a whole range efficiently, which is why B‑trees are the default choice for most columns.

### Hash index  

A **hash** index works like a very fast locker system. Each key is run through a *hash function* – a mathematical recipe that turns the key into a number called a *hash value*. That number tells the database exactly which “locker” (bucket) holds the row. If two different keys produce the same hash value, they end up in the same bucket, and the database must check each entry in that bucket to find the right one.

The advantage is that, for an equality test, the database can go directly to the bucket in **O(1)** time – essentially constant time, regardless of how many rows exist.

> **Note:** A hash index can only help with exact‑match queries (`=`). It cannot be used for range queries (`>`, `<`, `BETWEEN`) because the hash function scrambles the order of the keys.

**When to use it:**  
- Columns that are searched only with `=` (e.g., looking up a user by a unique token)  
- Very large tables where the hash function distributes rows evenly, keeping each bucket small  

If the data changes a lot, the hash table may need to be rebuilt to keep the buckets balanced, which can add overhead.

### Bitmap index  

A **bitmap** index stores a series of bits (0 or 1) for each distinct value of a column. Imagine a spreadsheet where each row is a person and each column is a possible value, such as “Male”, “Female”, “Student”, “Employee”. For the column “Student”, the bitmap would have a 1 in the position of every row that represents a student and a 0 elsewhere.  

When you ask the database for rows that satisfy a condition, it simply reads the relevant bitmaps and performs fast bitwise operations (AND, OR, NOT) to combine them. This is extremely efficient when the column has **low cardinality** – that is, only a few different values compared to the total number of rows.

> **In daily life:** Think of a light‑switch panel where each switch controls a specific group of lights. Turning a switch on (setting a bit to 1) instantly tells you which lights are lit, without scanning each bulb individually.

**When to use it:**  
- Columns with few distinct values (e.g., gender, status flags, boolean fields)  
- Data warehouses where queries often combine many such columns (`WHERE gender = 'F' AND status = 'Active'`)  

Bitmap indexes are not good for columns with many distinct values (high cardinality) because the bitmaps become large and waste space.

### Choosing the right kind  

Each index type balances speed of reads against cost of writes and storage:

| Index type | Best for | Not good for |
|------------|----------|--------------|
| B‑tree     | Equality, range, sorting | Very high‑frequency inserts/updates on the indexed column |
| Hash       | Pure equality lookups | Range queries, ordering, frequent changes |
| Bitmap     | Low‑cardinality columns, analytical queries | High‑cardinality columns, OLTP systems with many writes |

> **Remember:** Pick the index that matches the most common way you will query the column. Using the wrong type can make the database slower, not faster.

sections.heading: When Indexes Slow Down Writes
sections.body:
When you add a new row to a table, the database does more than just write that row into the main data file.  
It also has to keep every index that involves the changed columns up‑to‑date. Think of an index as a separate, sorted list that points back to the rows in the table. Whenever the table changes, the list must change too.

> **Definition:** An *index* is a data structure (often a B‑tree) that stores copies of one or more column values in sorted order, together with pointers to the rows that contain those values.

### Why a write becomes slower

1. **Locate the right place in the index** – The index is kept sorted, so the system must search the index to find where the new entry belongs. This search is fast (logarithmic time), but it still costs CPU cycles.

2. **Insert the entry** – After the spot is found, the database must actually insert the new key and pointer. In a B‑tree this may involve splitting a node, updating parent nodes, and possibly writing several pages to disk.

3. **Update related metadata** – The index stores information such as the number of entries, high‑water marks, and page free space. All of these must be adjusted.

If you perform an **UPDATE** that changes a column used in an index, the database may have to delete the old key from the index and insert a new key. A **DELETE** removes the key from the index entirely. Each of these steps repeats the work described above.

> **Note:** The extra work is proportional to the number of indexes that reference the changed columns. One index adds a small overhead; five indexes can make the same write several times slower.

### Everyday comparison

Imagine a library that keeps a master list of all books (the table) and also maintains separate alphabetical lists for each genre (the indexes). When a new book arrives, the librarian not only places the book on the shelf but also writes its title on every genre list that applies. If the book belongs to three genres, the librarian must make three entries. If the book later changes genre, the librarian must cross out the old entry and write a new one on the appropriate list. The more lists the librarian has to maintain, the longer it takes to process each new or changed book.

### What this means for performance

- **Write‑heavy workloads** (many INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE statements) feel the impact more strongly.  
- **Read‑heavy workloads** (mostly SELECT) benefit from indexes, because the extra cost is paid only once during the write, but many reads can use the fast lookup.  
- The trade‑off is a classic *read‑vs‑write* balance: more indexes improve read speed but increase write cost.

> **In daily life:** Think of a grocery store that keeps a price tag on every item (the table) and also a separate “sale” board for each department (indexes). Adding a new item means updating the price tag **and** the appropriate sale boards. The more boards you have, the longer it takes to stock the shelf.

### How the database mitigates the cost

Modern DBMSs use techniques such as:

- **Write‑ahead logging** – changes are first recorded in a fast log file, then applied to indexes in the background.  
- **Batching** – multiple index updates are combined into a single disk write.  
- **Deferred index maintenance** – some systems allow you to postpone index updates until a later “maintenance window.”

These tricks reduce the apparent slowdown, but the fundamental fact remains: every write must touch every relevant index.

> **Common mistake:** Assuming that adding an index only helps SELECT statements and has no effect on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE. In reality, each write pays the price of maintaining every index that involves the changed columns.

### Bottom line

When you design a table, add indexes only for columns that are searched or sorted frequently. If a column is rarely used in queries but is updated often, an index on that column will likely hurt more than it helps. Balancing the number and type of indexes is essential for a healthy database that performs well for both reads and writes.

sections.heading: Choosing Good Indexes
sections.body:
When you decide which columns should have an index, think of the index as a **shortcut map** that lets the database find rows quickly, but only if the shortcut points to places you actually look up often.

> **Definition:** *Selectivity* is a measure of how many different values a column contains compared to the total number of rows. A column with high selectivity has many distinct values (for example, a column of social‑security numbers), while a column with low selectivity has few distinct values (for example, a column that only stores “yes” or “no”).

Why does selectivity matter?  
If a column has many different values, an index can narrow the search down to a very small set of rows. Imagine a library where each book has a unique ISBN. If you have a list sorted by ISBN, you can jump straight to the exact book you need. In contrast, if the list is sorted by “genre” and you look for a specific title, you still have to scan many entries because many books share the same genre. The same principle applies inside a database: an index on a highly selective column lets the engine skip most rows and go directly to the few that match.

> **In daily life:** Think of a phone contact list. If you sort contacts by last name, finding “Zhang” is fast because few names start with Z. Sorting by “city” would be slower if many contacts live in the same city.

### Look for the columns that appear in queries

When you write a query, the database examines three main parts:

1. **WHERE clause** – conditions that filter rows (e.g., `WHERE country = 'Canada'`).
2. **JOIN condition** – how tables are linked together (e.g., `ON orders.customer_id = customers.id`).
3. **ORDER BY / GROUP BY** – how the result set is sorted or grouped (e.g., `ORDER BY purchase_date`).

If a column is used in any of these places, the database may benefit from an index on that column. The index can help:

- **Locate** the rows that satisfy the `WHERE` condition.
- **Match** rows between tables during a `JOIN`.
- **Retrieve** rows already in the required order, avoiding an extra sort step.

### Balance against write workload

Every time a row is inserted, updated, or deleted, the database must also modify any indexes that involve the affected columns. This extra work can slow down write operations. Therefore, before adding an index, ask:

- **How often does the table receive writes?**  
  A table that is updated thousands of times per second (e.g., a real‑time sensor log) should have very few indexes, otherwise each write would have to touch many index structures.
- **How many queries will benefit?**  
  If only a handful of queries use a column, the cost of maintaining the index may outweigh the speed gain for those queries.

> **Remember:** An index is a trade‑off: it speeds up reads but adds overhead to writes. Choose indexes where the read benefit is clearly larger than the write cost.

### Practical checklist for picking good indexes

1. **High selectivity** – Prefer columns with many distinct values.  
   *Example:* `email_address`, `order_number`, `product_sku`.
2. **Frequent use in WHERE/JOIN/ORDER BY** – Scan your most common queries; any column that appears repeatedly in these clauses is a candidate.  
   *Tip:* Use the database’s query‑analysis tools (e.g., `EXPLAIN` in MySQL) to see which columns cause full table scans.
3. **Low write frequency** – If a table is mostly read‑only (e.g., a reference table of countries), you can afford more indexes.  
   *Contrast:* A transaction table that records every purchase may need only a few essential indexes.
4. **Composite indexes for multi‑column filters** – When queries filter on several columns together, a single index that covers all those columns can be more efficient than separate single‑column indexes. The order of columns in a composite index matters: put the most selective column first.  
   $$\text{Composite index order} = \text{most selective column} \rightarrow \text{next most selective} \rightarrow \dots$$
5. **Covering indexes** – If an index contains all columns needed by a query (both for filtering and for the SELECT list), the database can satisfy the query using only the index, without touching the main table. This is especially useful for reporting queries that read many rows but only a few columns.

### When to stop adding indexes

- **Redundant indexes** – Two indexes that start with the same column(s) provide overlapping benefits; keep only the more useful one.
- **Very low selectivity** – Indexes on columns like `status` with values “active/inactive” rarely help because each value matches a large fraction of rows.
- **High write impact** – If adding an index makes insert or update latency exceed your performance target, reconsider its necessity.

By following these steps—checking selectivity, matching query patterns, and weighing read versus write costs—you can choose indexes that make your database fast for the most important operations while keeping maintenance overhead low.

sections.heading: Practical Example: Index Decision Process
sections.body:
Imagine you have a library and you want to find every book written by *J.K. Rowling* that was published after 2010.  
If the books are just piled on a shelf in no particular order, you would have to look at each book one by one until you find the ones you need.  
That is exactly what a database does when it has **no index** on the columns you are searching for: it scans every row, a process called a *full table scan*.

Now picture a card catalog that lists every author’s name together with the shelf location of each of their books.  
When you look up “Rowling” in the catalog, you instantly see the exact shelves to visit.  
That catalog is the analogue of a **database index** – a small, ordered structure that points to the rows that satisfy a condition, allowing the database to skip the irrelevant rows.

Below is a step‑by‑step walk‑through of how a developer decides whether to create such an index for a particular query.

---

### Step 1 – Write down the query you care about  

```sql
SELECT order_id, total
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 12345
  AND order_date >= '2023-01-01';
```

The query asks for all orders placed by a specific customer after a certain date.  
The columns that appear in the `WHERE` clause (`customer_id` and `order_date`) are the ones we might want to index.

> **Definition:** *Selectivity* is the fraction of rows that satisfy a condition.  
> A highly selective condition (small fraction) is a good candidate for an index because the index can quickly narrow the search.

### Step 2 – Estimate the selectivity of each condition  

1. **customer_id = 12345**  
   Suppose the `orders` table has 10 million rows and there are about 100 000 distinct customers.  
   On average each customer has 100 orders, so the condition will return roughly 100 rows.  

   $$\text{Selectivity}_{\text{customer}} = \frac{100}{10\,000\,000}=0.00001$$  

2. **order_date >= '2023-01-01'**  
   If the table contains three years of data, about one‑third of the rows (≈3.3 million) meet this date condition.  

   $$\text{Selectivity}_{\text{date}} = \frac{3\,300\,000}{10\,000\,000}=0.33$$  

The combined selectivity (both conditions true) is roughly the product of the two, because the conditions are independent:

$$\text{Selectivity}_{\text{combined}} \approx 0.00001 \times 0.33 = 0.0000033$$  

That means only about 33 rows are expected to be returned.

> **Note:** The product rule works best when the columns are not strongly correlated. If they are, you need actual statistics from the DBMS.

### Step 3 – Compare the estimated result size with the cost of scanning  

A full table scan would read all 10 million rows.  
Reading an index that points directly to the 33 matching rows would require far fewer I/O operations.  
Therefore, the index is likely to give a big speed‑up for this **read‑heavy** query.

### Step 4 – Choose the index type  

Because the query filters on two columns, we have two main options:

* **Single‑column index on `customer_id`** – the database can quickly find the 100 rows for that customer, then apply the date filter.
* **Composite (multi‑column) index on `(customer_id, order_date)`** – the index is already ordered by both columns, so the engine can jump straight to the first row with `customer_id = 12345` and `order_date >= '2023-01-01'`, returning only the 33 rows.

In this case the composite index is preferable because it eliminates the extra filtering step.

### Step 5 – Consider write‑side impact  

Every time a new order is inserted, the index must be updated.  
If the `orders` table receives thousands of inserts per second, the extra work could become noticeable.  
However, if inserts are modest (e.g., a few hundred per second) and the query is run many times per minute, the read benefit outweighs the write cost.

> **Common mistake:** Adding an index just because a column appears in a `WHERE` clause, without checking selectivity. Indexes on low‑selectivity columns (e.g., a boolean flag that is true for 90 % of rows) often do not help and only slow down writes.

### Step 6 – Make the decision and implement  

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_date
ON orders (customer_id, order_date);
```

After creating the index, you can verify its usefulness with the `EXPLAIN` command, which shows the query plan the database will use. If the plan now uses `idx_orders_cust_date` and shows a dramatically lower estimated cost, the decision was successful.

> **Remember:** Always test with real data and monitor both query latency and write throughput after adding an index. Adjust or drop the index if the performance gain is not as expected.

sections.heading: Common Pitfalls and Maintenance
sections.body:
When you add an index to a table you are creating a **shortcut** that the database can follow instead of scanning every row.  
That shortcut is very helpful for reading data, but it also costs something: the database must keep the shortcut up‑to‑date every time a row is inserted, updated, or deleted. If you are not careful, the shortcut itself can become a problem.

> **Common mistake:** Adding an index to every column that looks useful, without thinking about how often the data changes.

### Over‑indexing

Imagine a library where every book has a separate card in three different catalogues: one sorted by title, one by author, and one by publication year. If the library adds a new book, the librarian must write three cards. The more catalogues there are, the more work each new book creates. In a database, each extra index is another catalogue that must be maintained.

- **Read benefit:** Queries that use the indexed column can find rows quickly.
- **Write cost:** Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` must also modify each index that involves the changed column.

If you have many indexes on a table that is updated frequently, the extra work can slow down those write operations dramatically. The database may spend more time updating indexes than actually storing the new data.

> **Remember:** An index is worth keeping only if the speed gain for reads outweighs the extra time spent on writes.

### Stale (out‑of‑date) indexes

Databases try to keep indexes consistent automatically, but sometimes the information the optimizer uses to choose a plan becomes **stale**. The optimizer is the part of the database that decides whether to use an index or not. It relies on **statistics**—small summaries that describe how many rows have certain values, how many distinct values exist, etc.

If the data in a table changes a lot and the statistics are not refreshed, the optimizer may think an index is very selective (covers few rows) when in reality it now matches many rows. It will then choose the index, causing the query to read many index entries and then fetch the full rows—a slower path than a simple table scan.

> **Note:** Running a command like `ANALYZE` (PostgreSQL) or `UPDATE STATISTICS` (SQL Server) tells the database to recompute these summaries.

### Index rebuilding

Over time, especially after many deletions or updates, the physical layout of an index can become fragmented. Think of a bookshelf where books are constantly taken out and put back in random spots; eventually you have gaps and the shelf is harder to scan quickly. In a B‑tree index (the most common type), fragmentation means more pages must be read to follow the tree, increasing I/O cost.

Rebuilding an index reorganizes its pages into a compact, ordered form. Most systems provide a command such as `REINDEX` (PostgreSQL) or `ALTER INDEX REBUILD` (SQL Server). Rebuilding can:

- Reduce the number of pages the database must read.
- Free space that was left unused after many deletions.
- Reset the index’s internal statistics (some systems do this automatically).

> **Definition:** *Fragmentation* is the condition where the logical order of data does not match its physical order on disk, causing extra work to read it.

### Practical checklist

1. **Audit indexes regularly** – list all indexes on a table and ask: *Do we really need this for our most common queries?*  
2. **Monitor write performance** – if inserts or updates become noticeably slower after adding an index, consider dropping it or consolidating several indexes into a composite one (an index on multiple columns).  
3. **Schedule statistics updates** – many databases can auto‑update statistics, but for very active tables you may need to run them more often.  
4. **Plan index rebuilds** – set a maintenance window (e.g., nightly) to rebuild heavily fragmented indexes, especially on tables with high delete‑update churn.

By keeping these points in mind, you avoid the trap of “more indexes = always better.” Instead, you treat indexes as carefully tended tools: add them where they give a clear read benefit, keep their information fresh, and tidy them up when they become messy. This balanced approach ensures your database stays fast for both reading and writing.

practice.q: What is a database index and how does it help retrieve rows faster?
practice.a: A database index is a separate data structure, often a B‑tree, that stores the values of one or more columns along with pointers to the rows where those values appear. When a query searches for a specific value, the database can look up the value in the index (which is ordered) instead of scanning every row in the table. This reduces the number of rows examined from potentially millions to just a few, making the search much faster.

practice.q: Why can having too many indexes hurt write performance?
practice.a: Each time a row is inserted, updated, or deleted, the database must also modify every index that includes the affected columns. More indexes mean more work for each write operation, so the overall time to complete inserts, updates, or deletes increases. Therefore, excessive indexes can slow down write‑heavy workloads.

practice.q: Compare a single‑column B‑tree index with a composite (multi‑column) index. When would you choose each?
practice.a: A single‑column B‑tree index orders rows by one column only. It is best when queries filter or sort on that single column. A composite index orders rows by the first column, then the second, and so on. It can be used for queries that filter on the first column alone, on both columns together, or that sort by the same column order. Choose a single‑column index for simple, frequent searches on one field. Choose a composite index when you often query using a combination of columns (e.g., WHERE first_name = ? AND last_name = ?) or need to support ordering by those columns together.

practice.q: A table “Orders” has columns (order_id, customer_id, order_date, total). The most common query is: SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE customer_id = ? AND order_date BETWEEN ? AND ?. Which index would give the best performance and why?
practice.a: Create a composite index on (customer_id, order_date). The index is ordered first by customer_id, then by order_date. The query can use the index to quickly locate all rows for the given customer_id and then efficiently range‑scan the order_date values within the specified interval. This avoids scanning rows for other customers and speeds up the date range filter.

practice.q: Explain how a covering index can eliminate the need to read the table data (a “heap”) for certain queries. Give an example query and the index definition that makes it a covering index.
practice.a: A covering index contains all the columns required by a query, so the database can satisfy the query using only the index pages. Because the index stores the needed column values, it never has to fetch the full row from the table (heap). Example: Query SELECT order_id, total FROM Orders WHERE customer_id = 123;. A covering index would be defined as CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_total ON Orders(customer_id, order_id, total);. The index is ordered by customer_id and stores order_id and total as included columns. When the query runs, the engine can locate matching entries in the index and read order_id and total directly from the index, skipping the table lookup.

practice.q: A database experiences heavy write traffic on a “LogEvents” table (columns: event_id, user_id, event_type, timestamp). An analyst wants fast queries on recent events per user: SELECT * FROM LogEvents WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 100. Propose an indexing strategy that balances read speed and write overhead, and justify your choice.
practice.a: Use a composite index on (user_id, timestamp DESC). Definition: CREATE INDEX idx_log_user_time ON LogEvents(user_id, timestamp DESC);. This index orders rows first by user_id, then by timestamp in descending order, so the query can directly retrieve the newest 100 rows for a given user without scanning the whole table. To limit write overhead, avoid adding extra indexes on other columns; the single composite index provides the needed read performance while keeping write cost low. If write performance still suffers, consider partitioning the table by time (e.g., monthly) so each insert affects only the current partition, further reducing index maintenance cost.

data.recap: An index is a separate, sorted data structure that lets a database find rows quickly without scanning the whole table. It works like a book's index or a phone‑book shortcut, turning O(N) scans into O(log N) lookups. While indexes speed up reads, they add overhead to writes because every index must be updated. Choosing good indexes depends on column selectivity and query patterns.

lessons.title: Database Design in Practice
lessons.focus: Designing a small database for a real problem, step by step

data.title: Database Design in Practice
data.summary: In this final lesson students will design a small, real‑world database from start to finish, applying all concepts learned earlier. They will see how each design decision impacts the final SQL implementation.
objectives: Identify the real‑world problem and define its data requirements
Create an Entity‑Relationship diagram for the problem
Convert the ER diagram into normalized relational tables
Write the CREATE TABLE statements for the design
Explain how the design supports typical queries
data.prerequisites: Students should already know basic relational concepts, how to write simple SQL queries, and the purpose of normalization.
why: Designing a database for a real problem shows how theory becomes a useful tool in business, research, or everyday apps. It helps students understand the impact of good design on data integrity and future maintenance.
A well‑designed database reduces errors, improves performance, and makes it easier to add new features, which are critical in real‑world projects where data grows over time.

sections.heading: 1. Choose a Real‑World Scenario
sections.body:
Imagine you are going to build a tiny computer system that keeps track of a **small online store** that sells a few kinds of handmade candles.  
Before any tables or code appear, you must first decide **what real‑world problem you are solving**. This step is called *choosing a real‑world scenario*. It is like picking a story before you write a book – the story tells you which characters, places, and events you need to describe.

Why start here?  
If you begin with a clear scenario, every later decision (what tables you need, how they link together, what rules you enforce) will have a sensible reason. It also helps you and anyone who reads your design to understand *why* the database exists.

> **Definition:** A *scenario* is a simple, familiar situation that you can describe in everyday language. It provides the context for the data you will store.

### Step 1 – Pick a familiar setting

For beginners, a **small online store** works well because most students have seen or used an online shop. The store sells candles, accepts orders, and ships them to customers. This gives us three natural groups of information:

1. **Products** – the candles you are selling.  
2. **Customers** – the people who buy the candles.  
3. **Orders** – the transactions that connect a customer to one or more products.

### Step 2 – List the information you need

Now write down, in plain sentences, everything you would like the store to remember. Think of the store as a notebook where you jot down details every time something happens.

**Products**  
- Each candle has a *name* (e.g., “Lavender Dream”).  
- It has a *price* (how much money a customer pays).  
- It belongs to a *category* (e.g., “Scented”, “Unscented”).  
- It may have a *stock quantity* (how many units are left in the warehouse).

**Customers**  
- Every customer has a *full name*.  
- They provide an *email address* for contact.  
- They give a *shipping address* where the candles will be delivered.  
- Optionally, a *phone number* for quick questions.

**Orders**  
- An order receives a unique *order number* so you can refer to it later.  
- It records the *date* the order was placed.  
- It stores the *total amount* (sum of all product prices in that order).  
- It links to the *customer* who placed it.  
- It lists the *products* ordered, together with the *quantity* of each product.

### Step 3 – Think about what changes over time

A good scenario also notes which pieces of information will change. For example:

- The *stock quantity* of a product decreases when an order is fulfilled.  
- A *customer’s address* might be updated if they move.  
- New *products* can be added, and old ones can be discontinued.

Recognizing these dynamics helps later when you decide how to enforce rules (called *constraints*) in the database.

> **In daily life:** Choosing a scenario is like deciding what you want to keep a diary about – you first pick the topic (travel, school, hobbies) before you start writing entries.

### Step 4 – Keep the list short and clear

Avoid the temptation to add every possible detail at once. For a first design, stick to the essentials listed above. Extra fields such as “discount code” or “gift wrap option” can be added later once the core structure works.

> **Common mistake:** Adding too many attributes at the beginning makes the design messy and hard to normalize later. Start simple, then expand.

### Step 5 – Summarize the scenario

Finally, write a brief paragraph that captures the whole picture. This will be the reference you return to when drawing the ER diagram or creating tables.

> **Remember:** A well‑chosen scenario is the foundation of a clean database. It tells you *who* (customers), *what* (products), and *how* (orders) – the three pillars you will model in the next steps.

sections.heading: 2. Identify Entities and Attributes
sections.body:
When we start to design a database we first have to decide **what things we want to store**.  
These “things” are called **entities**. An entity is simply an object or concept that is important for the problem we are solving – for example a *student*, a *course*, or a *library book*.  

> **Definition:** An **entity** is a distinct object or concept that we want to keep information about in the database.

Each entity has **attributes**. An attribute is a single piece of information that describes the entity, like a student’s name or a book’s ISBN. Think of an entity as a real‑world object and its attributes as the labels on a name‑tag you would stick on that object.

### Step‑by‑step way to find entities and attributes

1. **Read the scenario carefully** and underline every noun that could be a thing we need to track.  
2. **Group similar nouns** together – they usually belong to the same entity.  
3. **Ask yourself:** “Do we need to store more than one piece of information about this thing?” If yes, the thing is an entity and each piece of information becomes an attribute.  
4. **Pick a primary key** for each entity. A primary key is a special attribute (or a combination of attributes) that uniquely identifies each record of that entity. It must never be duplicated.

> **Note:** The primary key is often a number that the system generates automatically (e.g., *StudentID*), because numbers are easy for computers to compare.

### Example: A Small Library System

Suppose the scenario is: *“The town library wants to keep track of its books, members, and the loans of books to members.”*  

From this sentence we can spot three obvious nouns that can become entities:

| Entity | Why it is an entity | Possible attributes |
|--------|--------------------|----------------------|
| **Book** | Each physical book is a separate item the library owns. | ISBN, Title, Author, Publisher, YearPublished, CopiesOwned |
| **Member** | People who borrow books. | MemberID, FirstName, LastName, Email, Phone, JoinDate |
| **Loan** | The act of giving a book to a member for a period of time. | LoanID, MemberID, ISBN, LoanDate, DueDate, ReturnDate |

#### Choosing primary keys

- For **Book**, the ISBN (International Standard Book Number) is already unique worldwide, so we can use **ISBN** as the primary key.  
- For **Member**, we create a system‑generated number called **MemberID**; no two members will have the same ID.  
- For **Loan**, each loan transaction needs its own identifier, so we add **LoanID**.  

> **In daily life:** Think of a library card number – it is the *MemberID*. No two cards have the same number, so the library can always tell who is who.

### Writing the attribute list

When we list attributes we separate the primary key from the others, because the key has a special role. A clear way to write this is:

```
Book (ISBN PK, Title, Author, Publisher, YearPublished, CopiesOwned)
Member (MemberID PK, FirstName, LastName, Email, Phone, JoinDate)
Loan (LoanID PK, MemberID FK, ISBN FK, LoanDate, DueDate, ReturnDate)
```

- **PK** means *primary key*.  
- **FK** means *foreign key* – an attribute that points to the primary key of another entity (here `MemberID` in *Loan* refers to the *Member* table, and `ISBN` in *Loan* refers to the *Book* table).  

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to mark foreign keys. Without them the database cannot enforce the connections between entities, and you may end up with a loan record that refers to a non‑existent member.

### Quick checklist for this step

- [ ] Have you listed every noun that represents a thing you need to store?  
- [ ] Does each entity have at least one attribute that can serve as a unique identifier?  
- [ ] Are all attributes written in singular form (e.g., *Title* not *Titles*)?  
- [ ] Have you noted which attributes are primary keys and which are ordinary fields?  

By the end of this stage you will have a clean table‑like description of every entity and its attributes, ready to be turned into an ER diagram and later into relational tables. This disciplined approach prevents later confusion and makes the whole design process much smoother.

sections.heading: 3. Define Relationships
sections.body:
When we have listed the entities (for example **Student**, **Course**, **Enrollment**) we must now describe how they are connected.  
A **relationship** tells us what can happen between two (or more) entities.  
Think of a relationship as a rule that says “when one thing exists, another thing may also exist, and they are linked together.”  

> **Definition:** A relationship is the logical connection between two entities that shows how instances of one entity are associated with instances of another entity.  

### 1. Types of cardinality  

The most important property of a relationship is its **cardinality** – the number of instances that can be linked on each side. There are three basic patterns:

| Cardinality | Meaning |
|-------------|---------|
| **One‑to‑one (1:1)** | Each instance of Entity A can be linked to **at most one** instance of Entity B, and vice‑versa. |
| **One‑to‑many (1:M)** | One instance of Entity A can be linked to **many** instances of Entity B, but each instance of B links back to **only one** A. |
| **Many‑to‑many (M:N)** | An instance of A can be linked to many B’s **and** a B can be linked to many A’s. |

Why does this matter? Knowing the cardinality tells us how to store the data efficiently and which **foreign key** columns we will need later.

> **In daily life:** Imagine a library. A *book* can have many *borrowers* over time (one‑to‑many), but each *borrower* can borrow many *books* (many‑to‑many). To record who borrowed what, we need a separate *Borrow* record that links the two.

### 2. Determining the correct cardinality  

Follow these steps for every pair of entities:

1. **Ask a question** about the real‑world rule.  
   - *Can a student have more than one address?* If the answer is “yes,” the relationship between **Student** and **Address** is one‑to‑many.  
2. **Check the opposite direction.**  
   - *Can an address belong to more than one student?* If the answer is “no,” we keep the one‑to‑many direction as described.  
3. **Look for many‑to‑many clues.**  
   - *Can a course have many students and can a student enroll in many courses?* Both answers are “yes,” so **Student** ↔ **Course** is many‑to‑many.  

If you are unsure, draw a small table of examples with made‑up data. Seeing the pattern often clears confusion.

> **Note:** A many‑to‑many relationship cannot be stored directly in a single relational table; it must be broken into two one‑to‑many relationships using a **junction (or associative) table**.

### 3. Introducing foreign keys  

A **foreign key** is a column (or set of columns) in one table that refers to the **primary key** of another table. It is the technical way we enforce the relationship we just described.

- In a one‑to‑many relationship, the **many** side gets the foreign key.  
  Example: The **Enrollment** table (many) will contain a `student_id` that points to the primary key `student_id` in the **Student** table.  

- In a one‑to‑one relationship, either side could hold the foreign key, but it is common to place it on the side that is optional.  
  Example: If every **Student** may have a **Locker**, the **Locker** table can store `student_id` as a foreign key, ensuring each locker belongs to at most one student.

- In a many‑to‑many relationship, the junction table holds two foreign keys, one for each participating entity.  
  Example: The **Enrollment** table will have `student_id` (FK to **Student**) **and** `course_id` (FK to **Course**).  

The foreign key not only links rows but also lets the database check that you do not create an invalid link (e.g., an enrollment that refers to a non‑existent student).

### 4. Writing the relationship in words  

After you have identified the cardinality, write a short sentence for each pair. This sentence becomes part of your design documentation and helps later when you draw the ER diagram.

- *A **Student** can enroll in many **Courses**, and a **Course** can have many **Students**.* → many‑to‑many, needs junction table **Enrollment** with foreign keys `student_id` and `course_id`.  
- *A **Course** is taught by one **Instructor**, but an **Instructor** can teach many **Courses**.* → one‑to‑many, foreign key `instructor_id` placed in **Course**.  
- *Each **Student** has exactly one **Profile**, and each **Profile** belongs to exactly one **Student**.* → one‑to‑one, foreign key `student_id` in **Profile**.

> **Common mistake:** Treating a many‑to‑many relationship as if you could put two foreign keys in one of the original tables. This creates duplicate data and makes updates error‑prone. Always use a separate junction table.

### 5. Quick checklist before moving on  

- [ ] Have you written a plain‑English description for every pair of entities?  
- [ ] Did you label the cardinality correctly (1:1, 1:M, M:N)?  
- [ ] Have you identified which side will hold the foreign key(s)?  
- [ ] For every many‑to‑many case, have you planned a junction table?  

When this checklist is complete, you are ready to draw the ER diagram (step 4) and later convert the design into relational tables. The clear definition of relationships now ensures that the database will faithfully represent the real‑world rules you started with.

sections.heading: 4. Draw an ER Diagram
sections.body:
When you have listed the entities, their attributes, and the way the entities are linked, the next step is to turn that information into a picture – an **Entity‑Relationship (ER) diagram**.  
Think of an ER diagram as a map of a city. The **entities** are the neighborhoods, the **attributes** are the street names inside each neighborhood, and the **relationships** are the roads that let you travel from one neighborhood to another. By drawing the map first, everyone can see the whole layout before any construction begins.

### 1. Choose the symbols

| Symbol | Meaning | How to draw it |
|--------|---------|----------------|
| **Rectangle** | An entity (a thing we want to store information about) | A plain box, write the entity name inside, usually in **singular** form (e.g., *Student*) |
| **Oval** | An attribute (a property of an entity) | A small ellipse attached to its entity with a straight line |
| **Underline** | Primary key (the attribute that uniquely identifies each record) | Write the attribute name inside the oval and underline it |
| **Diamond** | A relationship (how two entities are connected) | A diamond shape placed between the related entities, label it with a verb phrase (e.g., *enrolls in*) |
| **Line** | Connection between symbols | Straight line; add a small “crow’s foot” (three short lines) at the many‑side of a relationship |
| **Double line** | Total participation (every instance of the entity must take part in the relationship) | Draw a double line on the side of the entity that is mandatory |

> **Definition:** *Primary key* – an attribute (or set of attributes) whose value is unique for every entity instance. It is the “ID badge” that lets the database tell one record from another.

### 2. Place the entities

Start by drawing a rectangle for each entity you identified in step 2. Write the entity name in the centre of the rectangle. If you have three entities – **Student**, **Course**, and **Instructor** – you will have three separate boxes on the page.

### 3. Add attributes

For each entity, list its attributes as ovals around the rectangle. Connect each oval to its rectangle with a straight line. Remember to underline the attribute that is the primary key:

- **Student**: *student_id* (underlined), name, email, birth_date  
- **Course**: *course_code* (underlined), title, credits  
- **Instructor**: *instructor_id* (underlined), name, office

If an attribute is **multivalued** (e.g., a student can have several phone numbers), draw a double oval around it. Most attributes are single‑valued, so a single oval is enough.

### 4. Draw the relationships

Identify how the entities interact:

- A **Student** *enrolls in* a **Course**.  
- An **Instructor** *teaches* a **Course**.

For each verb phrase, draw a diamond and write the phrase inside. Connect the diamond to the related entities with lines. At the end of each line, add the appropriate cardinality:

- Near **Student** side of *enrolls in*, draw a crow’s foot to show “many” (a student can enroll in many courses).  
- Near **Course** side, draw a single line (a course can have many students, but each enrollment links one student to one course).

If a relationship is **mandatory** for an entity (e.g., every *Course* must have at least one *Instructor*), use a double line on the **Course** side of the *teaches* relationship.

> **In daily life:** Think of a school timetable. Each class (Course) must have a teacher (Instructor) and many students attend it. The timetable is the visual representation of those connections, just like the ER diagram shows them on paper.

### 5. Check for completeness

Walk through the diagram and ask:

- Does every entity have at least one attribute?  
- Is the primary key underlined?  
- Are all relationships labeled with a clear verb phrase?  
- Do the crow’s feet correctly reflect “one‑to‑many” or “many‑to‑many” connections?

If you spot a missing line or an attribute, add it now. It is easier to edit the sketch than to discover a problem later when you start building tables.

### 6. Optional: Add weak entities or associative entities

Sometimes a relationship itself has attributes (e.g., *Enrollment* might store the *grade*). In that case, treat the relationship as an **associative entity**: draw a rectangle for *Enrollment*, give it its own attributes, and connect it to the original entities with one‑to‑many lines. This step is not always needed, but it keeps the diagram tidy when extra data belongs to the link rather than to either side alone.

> **Common mistake:** Drawing a many‑to‑many line directly between two entities without an associative entity. This hides the attributes that belong to the relationship and makes later normalization harder.

### 7. Final look

Your finished ER diagram should look like a clean city map: rectangles for neighborhoods, ovals for street names, diamonds for roads, and clear symbols showing where traffic flows. Keep the layout simple – avoid crossing lines when possible, and space the entities evenly. A clear diagram helps everyone (including future programmers) understand the structure before any code is written.

> **Remember:** An ER diagram is a communication tool, not a final product. Its purpose is to make the database design visible and understandable, just as a blueprint helps builders see the house before laying the foundation.

sections.heading: 5. Normalize the Design
sections.body:
When we first draw tables from an ER diagram we often end up with columns that repeat the same information or that depend on each other in a hidden way.  
Normalization is a systematic way to clean those tables so that each piece of data lives in exactly one place. By doing this we avoid **redundancy** (the same fact written many times) and **update anomalies** (situations where changing a fact in one row does not automatically change it everywhere it should).

> **Definition:** *Normalization* is the process of organizing a relational database according to a series of rules called normal forms. Each normal form removes a specific type of problem.

### First Normal Form (1NF)

A table is in **First Normal Form** when every column holds only *atomic* values – that is, a single, indivisible piece of data – and each row is unique.

*Why it matters:* Imagine a table of students that stores the courses a student takes in one column as a list: `Courses = "Math, English, History"`. If we want to find all students taking *English*, we would have to search inside a string, which is slow and error‑prone. By splitting the list so that each row contains only one course, the data becomes easier to query and update.

**Steps to achieve 1NF**
1. Identify any column that contains multiple values or repeating groups.  
2. Create a new row for each individual value, keeping the other columns the same.  
3. Add a primary key (a column or set of columns that uniquely identifies each row) if one does not already exist.

### Second Normal Form (2NF)

A table that is already in 1NF reaches **Second Normal Form** when every non‑key column is *fully dependent* on the whole primary key, not just part of it.

*Why it matters:* Consider a table `Enrollments` with a composite primary key `(StudentID, CourseID)`. If we also store `StudentName` in this table, the name depends only on `StudentID`, not on the combination of `StudentID` and `CourseID`. If a student changes their name, we would have to update many rows – a classic update anomaly.

**Steps to achieve 2NF**
1. Make sure the table is already in 1NF.  
2. Look at each non‑key column and ask: *Does this column need the whole primary key to be identified?*  
3. If a column depends on only part of a composite key, move it to a new table whose primary key is that part.  
4. Keep the original table for the data that truly needs the full key.

### Third Normal Form (3NF)

A table is in **Third Normal Form** when it is in 2NF and no non‑key column depends on another non‑key column. In other words, every non‑key column must be directly dependent on the primary key, not indirectly through another column.

*Why it matters:* Suppose we have a `Products` table with columns `ProductID`, `CategoryID`, and `CategoryName`. `CategoryName` depends on `CategoryID`, not on `ProductID`. If the name of a category changes, we would have to update every product that belongs to that category – another update anomaly.

**Steps to achieve 3NF**
1. Ensure the table is already in 2NF.  
2. For each non‑key column, check whether it is dependent on another non‑key column.  
3. If such a dependency exists, create a separate table for the dependent group. The new table’s primary key will be the column that other columns depend on (e.g., `CategoryID`).  
4. Replace the dependent columns in the original table with a foreign key that references the new table.

> **In daily life:** Think of a phone book. In a poorly organized book you might write a person’s address next to every phone number they have. If the person moves, you must rewrite every line. Normalization is like keeping the address in one place and just pointing to it from each phone‑number entry.

### Putting It All Together

Let’s walk through a tiny example. After drawing the ER diagram for a library, we might start with this table:

| BorrowID (PK) | MemberID | MemberName | BookID | BookTitle | BorrowDate |
|---------------|----------|------------|--------|-----------|------------|

1. **1NF:** No column has multiple values, so we are fine.  
2. **2NF:** The primary key is `BorrowID`. `MemberName` depends only on `MemberID`, not on `BorrowID`. Move `MemberName` to a `Members` table:  

   **Members**  
   | MemberID (PK) | MemberName |

   The original table now keeps only `BorrowID`, `MemberID`, `BookID`, `BorrowDate`.  

3. **3NF:** `BookTitle` depends on `BookID`. Create a `Books` table:  

   **Books**  
   | BookID (PK) | BookTitle |

   The borrowing table now contains only foreign keys (`MemberID`, `BookID`) and the date.

The final set of tables is free of redundancy, and any change to a member’s name or a book’s title needs to be made in just one place.

> **Remember:** Normalization is a step‑by‑step cleaning process – 1NF removes repeating groups, 2NF removes partial dependencies, and 3NF removes transitive dependencies. Following these steps keeps your database tidy, fast, and safe from accidental inconsistencies.

sections.heading: 6. Translate to Relational Tables
sections.body:
Now that you have your Entity-Relationship (ER) diagram, you have a visual map of your data. However, a computer cannot "read" a drawing. You must translate that map into relational tables. A relational table is a grid of rows and columns where data is organized so that different tables can be linked together.

Think of this process like moving from a sketch of a house to a detailed blueprint. The sketch shows where the rooms are, but the blueprint tells the builder exactly where the pipes and wires go.

The first step is to turn every **Entity** (the "objects" in your diagram, like *Student* or *Course*) into its own table. The name of the entity becomes the name of the table. Every **Attribute** (the details about the entity, like *Student Name* or *Email*) becomes a column in that table.

> **Definition:** A Primary Key is a unique identifier for every row in a table. It ensures that no two records are exactly the same.

Every table must have one Primary Key. For example, in a *Student* table, you would not use the student's name as the key because two people might be named "John Smith." Instead, you use a unique ID number, such as `StudentID`.

Next, we must handle the **Relationships** (the lines connecting your entities). In a relational database, we do not draw lines. Instead, we use a **Foreign Key**. A Foreign Key is a column in one table that stores the Primary Key of another table. This creates a link between them.

> **In daily life:** Imagine a library. The "Book" table has a `BookID`. The "Loan" table records who borrowed the book. Instead of writing the whole book title and author again in the Loan table, the librarian just writes the `BookID`. That ID acts as a pointer back to the Book table.

How you place the Foreign Key depends on the type of relationship:

1. **One-to-Many:** This is the most common type. For example, one *Department* has many *Professors*. To link them, you place the Primary Key of the "One" side (Department) into the table of the "Many" side (Professor). Now, each professor row contains a `DeptID` showing where they work.

2. **Many-to-Many:** For example, one *Student* can take many *Courses*, and one *Course* has many *Students*. You cannot put a Foreign Key in either table because it would require storing a list of values in a single cell, which is not allowed. Instead, you create a new "Join Table" (also called a Junction Table). This table contains only two columns: the Primary Key of the Student and the Primary Key of the Course.

> **Common mistake:** Do not forget to define the data type for each column. A `StudentID` should be an integer, while a `StudentName` should be a string of characters (often called VARCHAR).

By following these steps, you transform a conceptual drawing into a logical structure. You now have a set of tables where every piece of data has a specific home and every relationship is tracked by a key.

> **Remember:** Every table needs a Primary Key, and every relationship needs a Foreign Key to connect the tables.

sections.heading: 7. Write CREATE TABLE Statements
sections.body:
Now that we have our design on paper, we need to tell the computer exactly how to build it. We do this using a language called SQL, which stands for Structured Query Language. This is the standard language used to communicate with almost all relational databases.

Think of a `CREATE TABLE` statement as a blueprint for a building. Before you can move furniture (data) into a room, you must first build the walls and define what each room is for. If you don't specify that a room is a "kitchen," you might accidentally try to put a bed in it. In a database, we define the "type" of data each column can hold so the computer can keep the information organized and clean.

> **Definition:** A Data Type is a label that tells the database what kind of information a column holds, such as text, whole numbers, or dates.

Let's look at our scenario. We will create three tables: `Students`, `Courses`, and `Enrollments`.

First, we create the `Students` table. We use `INT` for whole numbers and `VARCHAR` for text. `VARCHAR` stands for "variable character," which is just a fancy way of saying "a string of text of varying length."

```sql
CREATE TABLE Students (
    StudentID INT PRIMARY KEY,
    FirstName VARCHAR(50),
    LastName VARCHAR(50),
    Email VARCHAR(100)
);
```

Next, we create the `Courses` table. Notice that we also assign a `PRIMARY KEY`. This is a unique identifier that ensures no two records are exactly the same.

> **In daily life:** A Primary Key is like your Social Security Number or a Student ID card; it is the one piece of information that belongs to only one person.

```sql
CREATE TABLE Courses (
    CourseID INT PRIMARY KEY,
    CourseName VARCHAR(100),
    Credits INT
);
```

Finally, we create the `Enrollments` table. This table is different because it connects the other two. It uses `FOREIGN KEYS`. A Foreign Key is a column that refers to the Primary Key of another table. This creates a link between the two.

> **Definition:** A Foreign Key is a column that ensures "referential integrity," meaning you cannot enroll a student in a course if that student or course does not actually exist in the database.

```sql
CREATE TABLE Enrollments (
    EnrollmentID INT PRIMARY KEY,
    StudentID INT,
    CourseID INT,
    EnrollmentDate DATE,
    FOREIGN KEY (StudentID) REFERENCES Students(StudentID),
    FOREIGN KEY (CourseID) REFERENCES Courses(CourseID)
);
```

When writing these statements, the order matters. You must create the "parent" tables (Students and Courses) before the "child" table (Enrollments). If you try to create the Enrollments table first, the database will get confused because the Foreign Keys have nothing to point to.

> **Common mistake:** Trying to create a table with a Foreign Key before creating the table that the key refers to. This will cause an error.

By following these steps, we move from a visual drawing to a living system. The database now knows that every student has a unique ID, every course has a name, and every enrollment links a specific student to a specific course.

practice.q: You are designing a database for a library. Identify two possible entities and two attributes for each.
practice.a: 1. Entity: Book. Attributes: Title, ISBN. 2. Entity: Member. Attributes: Name, MemberID.

practice.q: Explain the difference between an entity and an attribute using a "Student" as an example.
practice.a: An entity is a real-world object or concept you want to store data about (e.g., the Student). An attribute is a specific piece of information that describes that entity (e.g., the Student's Date of Birth).

practice.q: In a school database, you have a "Teacher" entity and a "Class" entity. Define the relationship between them and specify if it is One-to-One, One-to-Many, or Many-to-Many.
practice.a: The relationship is "Teaches." It is typically One-to-Many because one teacher can teach many different classes, but each specific class is usually assigned to only one primary teacher.

practice.q: Why is normalization important when translating an ER diagram into relational tables?
practice.a: Normalization is important because it removes redundant data (duplicate information) and prevents data anomalies. For example, it ensures that if a customer changes their address, you only have to update it in one place rather than in every single order record.

practice.q: You have a table "Orders" with the following columns: OrderID, CustomerName, CustomerAddress, ProductID, and Quantity. Explain why this table is not normalized and how to fix it.
practice.a: This table is not normalized because it mixes Order data with Customer data. If a customer makes ten orders, their name and address are repeated ten times. To fix this: 1. Create a "Customers" table (CustomerID, CustomerName, CustomerAddress). 2. Create an "Orders" table (OrderID, CustomerID, ProductID, Quantity). Use CustomerID as a foreign key to link them.

practice.q: Translate the following scenario into a SQL CREATE TABLE statement: A "Products" table with a unique ProductID (integer), a ProductName (text), and a Price (decimal).

data.recap: This lesson guides students through the practical process of database design, from choosing a real-world scenario to writing SQL code. It covers identifying entities and attributes, defining relationships with cardinality, and visualizing the structure using ER diagrams. Finally, it explains how to refine the design through normalization and translate it into physical relational tables using CREATE TABLE statements.

key_terms.meaning: A simple, familiar situation described in everyday language that provides the context for the data to be stored.
A distinct object or concept, such as a person or place, that we want to keep information about in a database.
A single piece of information that describes a specific property of an entity.
A logical connection between two entities showing how they are associated with one another.
The number of instances of one entity that can be linked to instances of another entity (e.g., 1:1, 1:N).
The process of organizing data to remove redundancy and prevent update anomalies.
A unique identifier for every row in a table, ensuring no two rows are identical.
A label that tells the database what kind of information a column holds, such as text or integers.

quiz.q: Why is it important to start with a real-world scenario?
options: To write the SQL code faster
To ensure every design decision has a sensible reason
To eliminate the need for primary keys
quiz.why: A scenario provides the context and purpose for all subsequent database decisions.

quiz.q: In database design, what is an 'attribute'?
options: A table that links two entities
A unique ID for a row
A property that describes an entity
quiz.why: Attributes are the specific details, like a name or date, that describe an entity.

quiz.q: Which symbol is used to represent an entity in an ER diagram?
quiz.why: Rectangles are used to represent entities, usually written in singular form.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of normalization?
options: To make the ER diagram look better
To remove redundancy and update anomalies
To increase the number of tables
To change data types to text
quiz.why: Normalization ensures each piece of data lives in exactly one place to prevent errors.

quiz.q: What does First Normal Form (1NF) require?
options: Every table must have at least ten columns
Every column must hold only atomic values
Every entity must be linked to another
The use of only one table for the whole scenario
quiz.why: 1NF requires that data be indivisible (atomic) and that each row be unique.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a Primary Key?
options: To define the data type of a column
To uniquely identify every row in a table
To draw the relationships in an ER diagram
quiz.why: A primary key ensures that each record in a table can be specifically identified.
